name: ASPCA
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the ASPCA works only in the United States (owners and their dogs, cats and horses).
summary: The ASPCA, the oldest US animal welfare charity, placed about 70,900 animals in homes in 2025 (including relocation from crowded shelters), treated 109,700 animals in its hospital and low-cost clinics, supported 129,200 spay/neuter surgeries, ran Animal Poison Control, rescued animals from disasters and cruelty cases, gave $29m in grants to shelters, trained vets and shelter staff, ran national adoption campaigns and won puppy-mill laws; this model covers all of that except its farm-animal work, which has its own model. At the site's defaults it comes to about 0.0001 years of healthy life per $1,000: care for one dog or cat at a time reaches few animals per dollar, and nearly all of the result is the life satisfaction of owners whose pets the low-cost clinics treat, feed or keep at home. The biggest uncertainty is that owners' gain and how much suffering each kind of care spares an animal, all our judgment, so the result is mostly uncertainty, spanning about three orders of magnitude; every branch is discounted for missing outcome data.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: ASPCA (shelters, veterinary care, neutering, cruelty and disaster response, grants, education and policy for dogs, cats and horses, 2025)

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

sections.title: In chicken pain days
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for every animal model. The shared SAD figures are Ambitious Impact's, which count each species' pain as a share of a person's with its own species weights. Here those weights come out and Rethink Priorities' go in, so every species is counted in days of a chicken's disabling pain. How a chicken compares with a person is the one animal slider.

rows.explainer: Our judgment: the accounts don't split the line. rows.label: Placements: animals given homes through adoption, foster, relocation and placement support, 2025

source.title: ASPCA Form 990 for 2025
source.quote: THE ASPCA HELPED MORE THAN 70,900 ANIMALS FIND SAFE AND HEALTHY HOMES THROUGH ADOPTION, FOSTER, RELOCATION, MEDICAL AND PLACEMENT SUPPORT

rows.explainer: Dogs, cats and some horses. Includes the nearly 29,000 animals the relocation programme moved from crowded shelters to places with more adopters (same schedule) and the Equine Transition & Adoption Center's horses.

rows.label: Placements: suffering averted per day of the animal's new life, in days of disabling pain
rows.explainer: Our judgment on Ambitious Impact's pain scale (disabling 1, hurtful 0.1, annoying 0.01), the same as for Dogs Trust's rehoming because the change is the same: a screened home with vet care against the likely alternative (a crowded shelter, the street, a home that gave the animal up, private resale) is about two hours of hurtful-level distress a day less plus untreated illness, 0.01 days of disabling pain a day, from 0.003 (animals whose alternative was a settled home) to 0.03 (animals with untreated illness or severe stress). An animal that would otherwise have been put down counts nothing either way: deaths are not suffering. Net of a relocated animal's transport stress and disease risk (a day or two of hurtful distress against years of the new life, under 0.1% of the gain). No study measures it.

rows.label: Placements: share of the count that are full placements
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the 2025 annual report describes the 70,000+ as helped through 'adoption, relocation, pre-adoption spay/neuter and other placement support', so some animals only had a pre-adoption surgery (already among the 129,200) or a smaller piece of help; 85%, 70% to 100%.

rows.label: Placements: years the animal's better life lasts

source.title: Teng et al. 2022, Life tables of annual life expectancy and mortality for companion dogs in the United Kingdom, Scientific Reports 12:6415
source.quote: life expectancy at age 0 was 11.23 [95% confidence interval (CI): 11.19–11.27] years

rows.explainer: Dogs live about 11 years from birth (VetCompass, the best cohort study; US and cat figures are similar), cats a little longer. Placed animals are mostly young (a judgment: about 1 to 4 years old), leaving about 8 years, times the share that stay in the new home: 6, from 3 (older animals and horses placed for a few years, returns) to 9.

rows.label: Placements: days of disabling pain spared per animal, discounted
rows.explainer: Every future year discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Placements: days of pain spared before adjustments
Placements: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as for Dogs Trust's rehoming (0.7): the effect is a reasoned guess, the count the ASPCA's own and not broken down.

rows.label: Placements: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as for Dogs Trust (30%): most animals would find some home through other shelters and rescues, though relocated animals come from shelters that are full (where the alternative is often euthanasia, which counts nothing here). 10% to 60%.

rows.label: Placements: the ASPCA's share of the resources beside partners, volunteers and others
rows.explainer: Our judgment: foster carers, receiving shelters for relocated animals and adopters' own costs; the ASPCA runs the transport, medical preparation and its own adoption centre. 80%, 60% to 95%.

rows.explainer: Its share beside partners, volunteers and others, times the share of the spending not paid by fees where the shelter and veterinary line pays.

rows.label: Placements: share of credit used
Placements: delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: Our judgment: some placements are returned or don't last (returns within months run at about a tenth in shelter studies); 90%, 80% to 100%.

rows.label: Placements: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): the ASPCA counts the animals but no study measures how much less they suffer; the effect is our judgment.

rows.label: Placements: all adjustments combined
Placements, side effect: fewer animals bred for sale, as a share of the branch's result
rows.explainer: Our judgment: some adopters would otherwise have bought a puppy or kitten, so fewer are bred, sparing breeding animals' and puppies' suffering in commercial breeding. 10%, 0 to 30%. A side effect, weighed by the shared slider.

Veterinary care: animals given veterinary or behavioural care, 2025

source.title: ASPCA Form 990 for 2025
source.page: Schedule O, Part III line 4a (Access to care)
source.quote: IN 2025, THE ASPCA PROVIDED EXPERT VETERINARY AND BEHAVIORAL CARE TO MORE THAN 109,700 ANIMALS

rows.explainer: The animal hospital in New York, community veterinary clinics in New York, Miami and Los Angeles, mobile clinics, shelter medicine and the behaviour rehabilitation centres. Animals spayed or neutered there may be among them; the neutering branch counts only the births averted, so the surgery's own effect on the animal is here.

rows.label: Veterinary care: days of disabling pain spared per animal treated
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as for treatment in the Dogs Trust model: a treated infection, injury, dental disease or behavioural crisis shortens weeks of hurtful pain (0.1 a day) to days; about a month of hurtful pain spared is 3 days of disabling pain, from 0.5 (vaccinations, check-ups) to 15 (surgery that ends weeks of severe pain). Spread over weeks, so not discounted.

rows.label: Veterinary care: days of pain spared before adjustments
Veterinary care: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as for treatment in the Dogs Trust model (0.7).

rows.label: Veterinary care: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Reference class: the Access to Veterinary Care Coalition's 2018 national survey (University of Tennessee, reported by the AVMA: https://www.avma.org/javma-news/2019-02-15/report-outlines-barriers-accessing-veterinary-care-possible-solutions) found that about 28% of US pet-owning households couldn't get the veterinary care their pets needed in the previous two years, cost being the barrier for 74% of sick-pet care; the community clinics select for those owners, while the hospital's clients (a small share of the fees) would more often be treated elsewhere. We put half the care as care that wouldn't otherwise have happened in time, 30% to 80%.

source.title: AVMA News, Report outlines barriers to accessing veterinary care, possible solutions (15 February 2019), on the Access to Veterinary Care Coalition's 2018 report
source.page: Headline and summary of the survey
source.quote: Report outlines barriers to accessing veterinary care, possible solutions

Poison control: animals whose care the hotline supported, 2025

source.title: ASPCA Form 990 for 2025

source.quote: SUPPORTING THE CARE OF MORE THAN 334,500 ANIMALS IN 2025 THROUGH EXPERT CONSULTATIONS INVOLVING POTENTIAL TOXIC EXPOSURES

rows.explainer: Calls from owners and vets about a possible poisoning, mostly dogs and cats.

rows.label: Poison control: days of disabling pain spared per animal
rows.explainer: Our judgment: most exposures are harmless or minor and the call mostly saves a needless vet visit; in some the right decontamination or antidote early spares days of vomiting, seizures or organ damage. 0.2 days of disabling pain an animal on average, 0.02 to 1. The owners' relief is counted in the people's rows (apc_owner_gain_share).

rows.label: Poison control: days of pain spared before adjustments
Poison control: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Our judgment: a hotline's effect on animals' outcomes is little studied; lower than direct treatment (0.6).

rows.label: Poison control: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment: vets have other references and a commercial hotline exists (Pet Poison Helpline), and owners' own vet would often manage the case anyway. 40%, 20% to 70%.

rows.label: Poison control: the ASPCA's share of the resources beside partners, volunteers and others
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the ASPCA's own toxicologists; partners (microchip and insurance companies that pay for some calls) add a little. Times the share not paid by fees.

rows.label: Poison control: the ASPCA's donors' share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Its share beside partners, volunteers and others, times the share of the spending not paid by fees where the shelter and veterinary line pays.

rows.label: Poison control: share of credit used
Poison control: delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: Our judgment: some owners don't follow the advice or can't reach a vet in time; 85%, from 70% (much advice ignored) to 100% (all followed), anchored on the 90% for direct treatment, lower because the hotline acts at one remove.

rows.label: Poison control: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): the ASPCA counts the animals but no study measures how much less they suffer; the effect is our judgment.

Spay/neuter surgeries the ASPCA performed or paid for, 2025

source.title: ASPCA Form 990 for 2025
source.page: Schedule O, Part III line 4a (Access to care)
source.quote: SUPPORTED MORE THAN 129,200 SPAY/NEUTER SURGERIES NATIONWIDE THROUGH ASPCA PROGRAMS, PARTNERSHIPS AND FUNDED CLINICS

rows.explainer: Nearly 80,000 free or low-cost surgeries in its own clinics and about 50,000 more by partners it funded (2025 annual report letter).

rows.label: Neutering: share of surgeries on females
rows.explainer: Our judgment: spay clinics see slightly more females than males; males averting births only through the females they would have mated is in the rebound row.

rows.label: Neutering: litters a year an unneutered female would have
rows.explainer: Our judgment, anchored on Nutter et al. 2004's free-roaming cats (TNR clinic and colony cohort) for cats, which can have two or three a year, and fewer for owned dogs and cats kept apart from males.

rows.label: Neutering: kittens or puppies per litter
rows.explainer: Our judgment: cats average three to four, dogs more, first litters fewer.

rows.label: Neutering: years the animal would have bred before being neutered or dying anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment: free-roaming cats live a few years; owned animals are often neutered later anyway (the counterfactual row takes the share that would be neutered soon).

rows.label: Neutering: births averted net of the population refilling
rows.explainer: Our judgment: where neutering coverage is low, the remaining animals breed more and survive better, refilling part of the gap; the ASPCA's high-volume clinics target areas of high shelter intake. 50%, 20% to 80%.

rows.label: Neutering: share of the births averted that would have been unowned or shelter animals
rows.explainer: Our judgment: surgeries on free-roaming and community cats (TNR) avert unowned lives; owned animals' unplanned litters are mostly rehomed, many through shelters, and only the unowned or homeless share counts here (an owned life is not counted as suffering spared).

rows.label: Neutering: unowned animals' births averted per surgery
rows.formula: neu_female_share * neu_litters_per_year * neu_young_per_litter * neu_breeding_years * neu_net_of_rebound * neu_unowned_share

rows.label: Neutering: share of free-roaming kittens that die before six months

source.title: Nutter, Levine and Stoskopf 2004, Reproductive capacity of free-roaming domestic cats and kitten survival rate, JAVMA 225(9):1399-1402
source.quote: 127 of 169 (75%) kittens died or disappeared before 6 months of age

rows.explainer: Kittens born to free-roaming cats in North Carolina; 60% to 85% for other places and for puppies.

rows.label: Neutering: days of disabling pain in a kitten or puppy that dies young
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as for Dogs Trust's free-roaming pups: disease, starvation and trauma (the commonest cause in Nutter et al.) over days to weeks.

rows.label: Neutering: days of disabling pain in the life of an unowned adult
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as for Dogs Trust's free-roaming dogs: injuries, parasites, infections, hunger and cold over a few years.

rows.label: Neutering: days of disabling pain in the life of an unowned animal that isn't born
Neutering: days of pain spared before adjustments
rows.explainer: The births come about a year later, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Neutering: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as for Dogs Trust's neutering (0.6): births averted come from population models, not a count.

rows.label: Neutering: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment: free or low-cost surgery reaches many owners who would not otherwise pay, but some would have neutered later at a private vet. 40%, 20% to 70%.

rows.label: Neutering: the ASPCA's share of the resources beside partners, volunteers and others
rows.explainer: Our judgment: about 80,000 surgeries in the ASPCA's own clinics, 50,000 by partners it part-funds (their own staff and other funders' money), trappers' unpaid time for community cats. 75%, times the share not paid by fees.

rows.label: Neutering: the ASPCA's donors' share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Its share beside partners, volunteers and others, times the share of the spending not paid by fees where the shelter and veterinary line pays.

rows.label: Neutering: share of credit used
Neutering: delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: Our judgment: a few surgeries are on animals that could not breed (old, already pregnant and aborted counted as averted).

rows.label: Neutering: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): the ASPCA counts the animals but no study measures how much less they suffer; the effect is our judgment.

Disaster response: animals helped in disasters and emergencies, 2025

source.title: ASPCA Form 990 for 2025
source.quote: HELPED MORE THAN 20,700 ANIMALS AFFECTED BY DISASTERS AND OTHER EMERGENCIES THROUGH RESCUE, RESPONSE AND RECOVERY EFFORTS

rows.explainer: Including the California wildfires (a $5m response and preparedness fund). The annual report puts this count as 'disasters, emergencies and suspected cruelty', so the branch counts it less the cruelty-case animals, which have their own branch.

rows.label: Disaster response: days of disabling pain spared per animal
rows.explainer: Our judgment: rescue, emergency sheltering and treatment spares days to weeks of hunger, injury and exposure; the same scale as treatment (3 days, 0.5 to 15). Spread over weeks, so not discounted.

rows.label: Pet food assistance: meals for animals, 2025

source.title: ASPCA Form 990 for 2025
source.quote: SUPPORTED THE DISTRIBUTION OF MORE THAN 2 MILLION MEALS TO ANIMALS IN NEED THROUGH PET FOOD ASSISTANCE AND DISASTER RESPONSE EFFORTS

rows.label: Pet food assistance: share of the meals that fed disaster animals
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the 2 million meals include food for animals in disaster response, already counted in the disaster branch; 20,700 animals fed twice a day for a couple of weeks would be about 0.6 million meals, but many were fed by partners. A quarter, 10% to 40%, taken off the food terms.

rows.label: Pet food assistance: meals per animal per day
rows.explainer: Our judgment, because dogs and cats are usually fed twice a day: 2, from 1 (a meal is a day's ration) to 3 (small portions); a higher figure means fewer animal-days fed.

rows.label: Pet food assistance: suffering averted per animal-day fed, in days of disabling pain
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the food goes to owners short of money and to animals in disasters; without it some animals go hungry for some days or are given up. About 0.01 days of disabling pain a day fed, as for a placement's daily gain, 0.002 to 0.04.

rows.label: Disaster response and pet food: days of pain spared before adjustments
rows.formula: (dis_animals_helped - crl_animals_helped) * dis_pain_days_per_animal + food_meals * (1 - food_disaster_share) / food_meals_per_pet_day * food_suffering_per_pet_day

rows.label: Disaster response and pet food: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as for veterinary care here and treatment in the Dogs Trust model (0.7), because the effect per animal is the same kind of reasoned guess about days of untreated suffering; 0.5 if most animals were not at much risk, 0.9 if the guess holds.

rows.label: Disaster response and pet food: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment: local shelters, emergency services and owners would have helped many of the animals. 50%.

rows.label: Disaster response and pet food: the ASPCA's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Our judgment: disaster response is shared with emergency services, local shelters and other national groups; food is often donated by pet-food companies. 50%, 30% to 80%.

rows.label: Disaster response and pet food: share of credit used
Disaster response and pet food: delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: Our judgment: some help reaches animals that were not at risk.

rows.label: Disaster response and pet food: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): the ASPCA counts the animals but no study measures how much less they suffer; the effect is our judgment.

rows.label: Disaster response and pet food: all adjustments combined
Disaster response and pet food: days of disabling pain spared
Cruelty response: animals the ASPCA supported in cruelty cases, 2025

source.title: ASPCA Form 990 for 2025
source.page: Schedule O, Part III line 4a (Freedom from mistreatment)
source.quote: IN 2025, THE ASPCA SUPPORTED MORE THAN 1,300 ANIMALS IN CRUELTY CASES INVOLVING NEGLECT, HOARDING AND ORGANIZED FIGHTING

rows.explainer: Animals seized from neglect, hoarding and dogfighting, cared for at the Cruelty Recovery Center, the Recovery & Rehabilitation Center and the Behavioral Rehabilitation Center, then placed.

rows.label: Cruelty response: suffering averted per day of the animal's life after rescue, in days of disabling pain
rows.explainer: Our judgment: neglected, hoarded or fighting animals live with untreated disease, injury, fear and hunger, much of the day at hurtful level; rescue removes most of it. 0.1 days of disabling pain a day (a hurtful day), 0.02 to 0.3.

rows.label: Cruelty response: years the animal would otherwise have stayed in the cruel conditions
rows.explainer: Our judgment: without the case most animals would have stayed until removed by others or dead; a few years at most.

rows.label: Cruelty response: suffering spared by prosecutions and training, as a share of the rescued animals'
rows.explainer: Our judgment: forensic evaluations, legal help in more than 500 cases and training for 3,800 police, prosecutors and officers lead to convictions and more cases found, sparing other animals. 30%, 0 to 100%: no study measures deterrence in animal cruelty.

rows.label: Cruelty response: days of pain spared before adjustments
Cruelty response: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as for placements (0.7), because the suffering removed is our reasoned guess from the conditions described in cruelty cases; 0.5 to 0.9 for how far it holds across neglect, hoarding and fighting cases.

rows.label: Cruelty response: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment: police and local agencies lead the cases and would often have acted, with local shelters taking the animals. 50%.

rows.label: Cruelty response: the ASPCA's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Our judgment: police, prosecutors and local shelters share the work. 50%.

rows.label: Cruelty response: share of credit used
Cruelty response: delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: Our judgment: a few cases end with animals returned to their owners or not removed at all; 90%, from 80% (more cases lost in court) to 100%.

rows.label: Cruelty response: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): the ASPCA counts the animals but no study measures how much less they suffer; the effect is our judgment.

rows.explainer: Our judgment from the grant purposes the ASPCA lists (disaster response, live-release, spay/neuter, surrender prevention, farm animals, horses; Form 990 Schedule I): the spay/neuter grants are inside the 129,200 surgeries and disaster grants inside the response branch, so only the rest counts here. rows.label: Grants for farm animals, 2025 (left to the farm-animal model)

source.title: ASPCA Form 990 for 2025
source.quote: VETERINARY ASSOCIATION FOR FARM ANIMAL WELFARE 333 WEST BROWN DEER RD. UNIT G #481, MILWAUKEE, WI 53217 93-1583316 501(C)(3) 48,660

rows.explainer: The Fund to End Factory Farming's $160,305 (ASPCA news, 2025 grantees), Food Animal Concerns Trust $72,000 and the Veterinary Association for Farm Animal Welfare $48,660 (Schedule I): their outcomes belong to the farm-animal model, so they come off the policy line's grants here.

rows.label: Grants: grant dollars per extra animal placed or kept in its home
rows.explainer: Our judgment: US shelters spend a few hundred dollars per animal taken in; a grant that adds capacity, staff or surrender-prevention help buys an extra live outcome for about $1,000, $300 (keeping a pet at home with a small grant) to $4,000 (building and staff).

rows.label: Grants: extra animals placed or kept in their homes
Grants: days of pain spared before adjustments
rows.explainer: Each extra live outcome is valued like a placement.

rows.label: Grants: evidence adjustment

Public education: extra adoptions a year from the ASPCA's campaigns (The Rescue Effect and other messaging)
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The ASPCA spends $90m on public education and communications (much of it mail and television that also raises funds) and reports reach, not results: 44 million website views, 19,000 media placements, 700,000 magazines (Form 990 Schedule O, line 4b). The Rescue Effect campaign aims to move people from buying to adopting. US shelters place about 4 million animals a year; we put the campaigns' share at a quarter of a percent, 10,000 a year, from 1,000 to 50,000.

People: share of the animals given veterinary care that have an owner
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the 109,700 were treated 'through its hospital, adoption center, community veterinary clinics, sheltering operations, rehabilitation facilities' (Form 990 Schedule O, line 4a); shelter, rehabilitation and relocation animals have no owner, while the community clinics and the hospital, most of the volume, serve owned pets. 75%, 55% to 90%.

rows.label: People: share of the owners helped (where the help wouldn't have come anyway) whose pet had a problem that weighed on them
rows.explainer: Our judgment, conditional on the help being counterfactual (that is vet_counterfactual_adj's question, anchored on the cost barrier). Anchor: the clinics' case mix, roughly half preventive (vaccinations, spay/neuter, check-ups, where the owner carries no burden) and half sick or injured animals. Half, 25% to 75%. Of owned animals only (vet_owned_share); the clinics' owners only (the other kinds of help take own_share_burdened_need).

rows.label: People: owners' wellbeing gap while a pet is sick or at risk, in standard deviations
rows.explainer: Our judgment from a reference class. Spitznagel et al. (Veterinary Record 2017) compared 119 owners of sick animals with 119 owners of healthy ones and found higher caregiver burden, stress and depression and lower quality of life (p<0.001), which at that sample size implies a gap of at least about 0.3 to 0.45 SD; they report scale scores, not effect sizes. A third of an SD, 0.1 (a mild worry) to 0.6.

source.title: Spitznagel et al. 2017, Caregiver burden in owners of a sick companion animal: a cross-sectional observational study, Veterinary Record 181(12)
source.quote: Caregiver burden in owners of a sick companion animal: a cross-sectional observational study

rows.label: People: years the burden lasts without the help
rows.explainer: Our judgment: an untreated illness, a hungry or at-risk pet, or a scare weighs on the owner for weeks to months: a tenth of a year, from 0.03 (about two weeks) to 0.3 (a long illness or a pet kept from surrender).

rows.label: People: life satisfaction gained by an owner whose pet is treated or kept, WELLBYs
rows.explainer: The gap in SDs, at the site's one rate of WELLBYs per SD-year (@wellby_factors.wellbys_per_sd_year), over the months it lasts; within a year, so not discounted. Adopters' own gain is counted as 0, as for Dogs Trust: studies of pet ownership find no consistent effect on wellbeing.

rows.label: People: days of pet food each household gets
rows.explainer: Our judgment: pet food banks and disaster distributions give a few weeks' food at a time, some households coming back; 30 days, 10 to 90.

rows.label: People: pets per household helped with food or in a disaster
rows.explainer: Our judgment: households with pets have on average more than one (US pet-ownership surveys put dogs and cats at about 1.5 to 2 per owning household); 1.6, 1.2 to 2.5. The food and disaster counts are of animals, so one owner per this many.

rows.label: People: share of owners given food, disaster, poison-control or grant help who faced a problem that weighed on them
rows.explainer: Our judgment: unlike the clinics, where half the visits are preventive, these kinds of help come when the owner is already in trouble (no money for food, a disaster, a suspected poisoning, a pet at risk of surrender); 90%, 70% to 100%.

rows.label: People: share of the disaster animals that have an owner
rows.explainer: Our judgment: in disasters the ASPCA shelters evacuated families' pets and rescues strays and shelter animals moved out of harm's way; half, 30% to 80%.

rows.label: People: a poison-control call's relief to an owner, as a share of a treated pet's
rows.explainer: Our judgment: a call settles an acute scare in minutes and often saves a vet bill, against weeks of worry over a sick pet; a tenth, 3% to 30%.

rows.label: People: share of the grants' extra outcomes that keep a pet with its owner
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the grant purposes include surrender-prevention programmes that help owners keep their pets (Form 990 Schedule I); the rest are shelter placements, whose adopters count 0. 30%, 10% to 50%.

rows.label: People: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step: no study measures the ASPCA's clients' life satisfaction; the gain is our judgment.

rows.label: WELLBYs for owners whose pets are treated, fed, rescued or kept at home
rows.formula: own_ls_gain * (own_share_eased * vet_animals_helped * vet_owned_share * vet_counterfactual_adj * vet_attribution_share * vet_implementation_adj + own_share_burdened_need * (food_meals * (1 - food_disaster_share) / food_meals_per_pet_day / food_days_per_household / pets_per_household * dis_counterfactual_adj * dis_attribution_share * dis_implementation_adj + (dis_animals_helped - crl_animals_helped) * dis_owned_share / pets_per_household * dis_counterfactual_adj * dis_attribution_share * dis_implementation_adj + apc_animals_helped * apc_owner_gain_share * apc_counterfactual_adj * apc_attribution_share * apc_implementation_adj + grt_outcomes * grt_kept_share * grt_counterfactual_adj * grt_attribution_share * grt_implementation_adj)) * people_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: Owners the work aims at (the ASPCA's 'keep pets and people together'), so not a side effect: owners of pets treated at the clinics and hospital, households given pet food, families whose pets were rescued or sheltered in disasters, callers to poison control and owners kept with their pets by surrender-prevention grants. Each carries its branch's counterfactual, credit and delivery.
